To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the costs of failed coalitionary behavior influence the nature of coalitions formed by species, and concessions granted by dominants are not a common feature of coalitionary interactions.

(a) species that form coalions to contest social rank will evolve to regularly form coalitions that bridge the ranks, whereas species that form coalitons to contest fecundity will evolve to form coalitions that include all coalition members in the same rank, and (b) dominant individuals will concede resources to subordintates only to ensure that another individual becomes a more attractive coalitionary target.

coalitionary behavior evolves to maximize the fitness of the coalition members; the costs inflicted upon members of failed all-up coalitions are more severe than the costs inflicted upon bridging coalition members; the benefits of coalitionary behavior outweigh the costs in most circumstances; the evolution of coalition formation is influenced by the type of costs inflicted upon members; and dominant individuals concede resources and rank to subordinates only when it is in the dominant individual's best interest.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of coalition formation and how it is shaped by ecological and social factors.
the evolution of coalition formation, a behavior that has received little theoretical attention, but is common in many species.
the evolution of coalition formation, and how different types of coalitionary behavior are selected by natural selection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the evolution of coalition behavior is a function of the type of cost that is inflicted upon members of failed coalitionary attempts, the type of cost being contested by coalitions (social rank versus fecundity), and the concessions made by dominant individuals to potential coalition targets.
coalitionary behavior is a highly flexible and context-specific behavior that has evolved to be highly adaptive to its ecological and social setting.
coalitionary behavior is a common evolutionary strategy that can emerge in a variety of social and ecological contexts.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the costs of coalition failure, and not the benefits of coalition formation, are most important in the evolution of coalition formation, and that concessions are not a common feature of coalitionary behavior.
the costs associated with forming coalitions and the concessions granted by dominant to prevent such coalitions are important factors in shaping coalitionary behavior in the wild.

the evolutionary consequences of coalitionary behavior are highly contingent upon the nature of the ecological and social conditions under which coalitions form, and the nature of costs incurred by members of failed coalitionary attacks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the costs of coalition failures can have a profound effect on the evolution of coalition behavior.
the nature of coalition costs and concessions are critical factors that determine how coalitionary behavior is likely to evolve in nature.

the costs of coalition formation are a major determinant of the type of coalitionary behavior observed in a given species, and that these costs may be influenced by the nature of the ecological and social setting.
